 If Your Social Security Is $1,800, Here’s What It Could Become in 2027
 Josh Koebert 2026년 11월 2일 월 오전 11:36 UTC 0 
If you're one of the millions of people collecting a Social Security check close to $1,800 a month, you've probably already heard that a raise is coming in 2027. The Social Security Administration (SSA) made it official in October, confirming the exact percentage that will apply to benefits starting in January.
But knowing the percentage and knowing what it means for your specific check are two different things. A general announcement doesn't tell you what shows up in your account, especially once Medicare premiums and any tax withholding come out. 
 Here's how to take that $1,800 figure and turn it into a real number, plus where to find your own personalized amount. And if your budget is already tight, there are ways that could help with bills if you're living on just Social Security .

 The 2027 COLA is 3.6%, confirmed by the SSA
The SSA announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027 , effective for Social Security benefits paid starting in January 2027, according to the agency's official announcement. The COLA is based on the increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) from the third quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026, as required under the Social Security Act.
This adjustment applies broadly. Nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see the increase in their January 2027 payments, and about 7.3 million people receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI) will see higher payments starting with the December 31, 2026 payment, per the SSA. That's because SSI's payment date shifts earlier when the 1st of the month falls on a holiday or weekend.

 Turning $1,800 into a real dollar figure
Here's the math behind the headline. If your current gross monthly Social Security benefit is $1,800, applying the 3.6% COLA works like this:
$1,800 x 0.036 = $64.80
$1,800 + $64.80 = $1,864.80
That puts the illustrative new gross benefit at $1,864.80 a month, an increase of $64.80. This is a straightforward example for a round number. Your own benefit almost certainly isn't exactly $1,800, so your dollar increase will be different, even though the same 3.6% applies to everyone's benefit.
It's also worth noting that the SSA rounds the monthly amount it pays down to the next lower whole dollar after any deductions, so a $1,864.80 benefit with nothing withheld would likely be paid as $1,864. Your personal COLA notice shows the official, rounded figure.
 This is your gross benefit, not necessarily your deposit
This is an easy part of the annual COLA increase to overlook. The $1,864.80 figure in the example above represents the gross benefit, the amount calculated before any deductions. It is not automatically the amount that lands in your bank account.
Many beneficiaries have their Medicare Part B premium deducted directly from their Social Security check. The standard Medicare Part B premium for 2026 is $202.90 a month, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). As of late October, CMS hadn't announced the standard 2027 Part B premium, which it typically releases in the fall.
If your premium increases for 2027, that increase could offset some or all of your COLA bump before you ever see it. Higher earners may also pay an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA) on top of the standard premium, which is generally based on the modified adjusted gross income on your tax return from two years earlier, according to the SSA.
Some beneficiaries also have federal income tax withheld voluntarily, or have deductions for things like Medicare Advantage or Part D drug plan premiums. None of these show up in the simple "gross benefit times COLA" math, which is why two people with the same starting benefit could see different amounts actually deposited.

 How your actual 2027 amount is calculated
Your primary insurance amount (PIA) is the benefit the SSA calculates from your 35 highest-earning years, adjusted for wage growth. Your PIA is what you'd receive at full retirement age, which is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later, according to the SSA.
If you claimed benefits early or delayed past full retirement age, the SSA reduces or increases your benefit, and subtracts any deductions, such as Medicare premiums. 
 Multiplying your current gross benefit by 1.036 gives a close estimate, but rounding at each step means your official amount could differ slightly.
For context on the range of outcomes, the SSA's 2027 COLA fact sheet shows the estimated average monthly benefit for all retired workers rising to $2,170 in January 2027, up from an estimated $2,095 before the COLA. 
 On the high end, a worker who earned the Social Security taxable maximum every year starting at age 22 and started benefits at age 70 in 2026 could receive $5,181 a month, according to the SSA. By comparison, the maximum benefit for someone retiring at full retirement age is lower, rising from $4,152 in 2026 to $4,188 in 2027, according to the SSA's 2027 COLA fact sheet.
 When the higher payment actually begins
Higher Social Security retirement and survivor benefits begin with payments made in January 2027, according to the SSA. SSI recipients see their increase slightly earlier, with the higher payment issued December 31, 2026, because SSI payments are normally made on the 1st of the month and shift earlier when that date falls on a weekend or holiday.
There's no action required to receive the increase. It's applied automatically to eligible beneficiaries' accounts based on SSA records.
 Where to find your exact personalized amount
Rather than estimating from a round number like $1,800, you can find your actual new benefit amount through the SSA's COLA notice. According to the SSA, beneficiaries with a personal my Social Security account can view their notice online starting in late November 2026. If you don't have an account yet, you'll need to create one and enroll in paperless notices by November 18 to see your notice online.
If you don't set up paperless notices, your COLA notice will arrive by mail in December 2026. The SSA says this is now a simplified, one-page notice written in plain, personalized language that spells out your exact new benefit amount, the effective date, and any deductions, such as Medicare premiums, being withheld. For Medicare enrollees, the 2027 premium amount will also be available through the my Social Security Message Center starting in late November 2026.
If you have questions after reviewing your notice, you can reach the SSA at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778).

 Bottom line
A $1,800 benefit becoming roughly $1,864.80 is a helpful way to visualize how the 2027 COLA works, but it's an illustration, not a prediction of what you'll personally see deposited. Your real number depends on your specific benefit, and what actually lands in your account depends on Medicare premiums, IRMAA, and any voluntary withholding you've set up.
The most reliable way to know your 2027 amount is to check your COLA notice directly through your my Social Security account or wait for the mailed version in December. Comparing that figure to your current deposit, not to a rough percentage calculation, will give you the clearest picture of what's actually changing in your budget next year. And if your check doesn't go as far as you'd like, a few simple moves could help you stretch your retirement dollars further .
 FAQs
 When will the 2027 Social Security increase start?
 The increase begins with Social Security payments received in January 2027. SSI recipients will receive their first increased payment on December 31, 2026, because January 1 is a federal holiday.
 Could the COLA make more of my Social Security benefits taxable?
 Yes. A higher benefit could push your "combined income" above the threshold where benefits become taxable or increase the portion subject to tax. Combined income includes your adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest, and half your Social Security benefits. Benefits may become taxable above $25,000 for single filers or $32,000 for married couples filing jointly.
 Does the COLA erase the reduction from claiming Social Security early?
 No. The COLA increases the benefit amount used in your calculation, but your early claiming adjustment still applies. You'll receive cost-of-living increases while continuing to receive a smaller monthly benefit than you would have received by waiting until full retirement age.
